title: He touched his ear (Luke 22:47–53)
hookLine: a disciple strikes a servant with a sword; Jesus heals the man's ear

lines: NIGHT ON THE MOUNT OF OLIVES.
A SWORD, AND A SERVANT'S EAR.
cards: Night on the Mount of Olives. Jesus is still speaking when a crowd arrives, and walking in front of them is Judas.
He comes close to kiss Jesus, and Jesus asks him quietly, in the King James words: "Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?" The disciples see what's happening.
Someone asks, Lord, shall we strike with the sword? Before anyone answers, one of them swings. The blade catches the high priest's servant and cuts off his right ear.
Blood on the ground, swords drawn in the dark, and everything about to get worse.

teach.b: Then Jesus speaks. The King James has: "Suffer ye thus far." The Greek is just a few words, and translators aren't sure how to put them: let them have their way, or no more of this, enough.
Either way, it's a word to stop.

teach.h: HE TOUCHED HIS EAR, AND HEALED HIM.
teach.b: Then a detail only Luke tells: "And he touched his ear, and healed him." Jesus is being arrested. His friends are panicking.
A night of trials and beatings is ahead.

teach.h: A HEALING FOR THE OTHER SIDE.
teach.b: And in the middle of his own arrest, he heals a man from the side that came to take him: not one of his own, but a servant on the other side, bleeding in the dark.

John's Gospel adds two names: the swordsman was Peter, and the servant was Malchus. Luke leaves them unnamed, and the scene works either way. Then Jesus turns to the chief priests, temple captains and elders who came out.
You came with swords and clubs, as if I were a robber. I was with you every day in the temple, and you didn't lift a hand.
"But this is your hour, and the power of darkness."

teach.h: AND HE TOUCHED HIS EAR, AND HEALED HIM.
teach.b: Christians have gone back to this scene when they argue about violence and faith. Some hear in it a call to refuse force entirely; others hear a limit on it. Both start from what Jesus did with his hands.

how: Christians remember the arrest during Holy Week, and some churches, such as the historic peace churches, return to scenes like this one when they teach about nonviolence.

o: the servant whose ear was cut off, then healed
the temple captain who led the arrest
the disciple who drew a sword in the garden

games.q: what's inside Luke 22:47–53 — tap the pairs.
p: cut off the servant's right ear

s: only Luke tells us Jesus healed the servant's ear
Matthew, Mark and John tell of the cut ear; only Luke tells of the healing.
Luke names the swordsman as Peter
Luke leaves him unnamed. John's Gospel names Peter, and the servant Malchus.
the man Jesus healed in the garden was one of his own disciples
it was the high priest's servant, from the side that came to arrest him.

games.q: you're in the garden. a friend has just cut off the ear of a man who came to arrest you. swords are out. what do you do?
o: stop the fight and heal the man's ear.
games.why: "suffer ye thus far. and he touched his ear, and healed him." the healing is for the man on the other side.

practice: Think back over this week, or this year, for something you damaged in a moment of heat: a sharp text, a slammed door, a friendship cut with one swing.
Picture it plainly, without beating yourself up, then picture one small thing that would begin to mend it, an apology, a call, paying for what you broke.
If you pray, ask God for the courage to do it; if you don't, simply choose the first step.

wordCard.voice: Malchus. The high priest's servant whose ear Peter cut off and Jesus healed, named only in John's Gospel, not Luke's.

orig.note: Greek: the ear, especially the outer ear. the word Luke uses when Jesus touches and heals it.

carryVoice: Your line: no more of this. A week from the end of the age to the upper room, the table, the garden and the arrest. Five hundred eighty-one days, and another week on the path.
